rows.label: Formula
rows.text:
$$\text{radial nodes}=n-l-1,\quad \text{angular nodes}=l,\quad \text{total}=n-1$$
$$\text{orbitals in a subshell}=2l+1;\qquad \text{capacity}=2(2l+1)$$
$$\mu=\sqrt{u(u+2)}\ \text{BM};\qquad \text{shell capacities }2,\ 8,\ 18,\ 32$$

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: ❌ Orbit and orbital mean the same thing. ✅ Orbit = fixed 2D path; orbital = 3D probability region.  ·  ❌ A p orbital has two lobes, so it holds two electrons in each lobe. ✅ The lobes together form one orbital, which holds a pair of electrons of opposite spin.

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: The most probable distance of the 1s electron is 0.529 Å (52.9 pm).  ·  A 2p orbital has one nodal plane through the nucleus; 3p has one nodal plane plus one radial node.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: **Problem:** Total nodes in a 3p orbital? **Solution:** radial = n − l − 1 = 1; angular = l = 1; total = n − 1 = 2.  ·  **Problem:** How many electrons fill all p orbitals of the n = 3 shell? **Solution:** 2l + 1 = 3 orbitals × 2 = 6 electrons.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: Covers only: orbitals, shape of s, p orbitals only (within Atomic Structure).  ·  Out of scope here: topics of neighbouring units in Chemistry — don't mix them.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ### 1. Meaning of an orbital  ·  An orbital is the three-dimensional region around the nucleus in which the probability of finding the electron is maximum (the ~90–95% boundary-surface region) for a given energy state. It comes from the wave function ψ of the Schrödinger equation, and |ψ|² is the probability density. An orbital has *no sharp boundary* and does not describe a path.

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Three p orbitals at 90° explain the 90° bond angle in H₂S (pure p bonding).  ·  answer pattern for "Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only": define → method → result. Structure earns the marks on 6–10 mark questions.

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: state + explain the main idea of "Orbitals and shape of s and p orbitals only" with one example.  ·  compare "Orbitals" with the related idea from a neighbouring unit.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Quote the node formulas (n − l − 1 radial, l angular) — a recurring numerical point.  ·  Describe orbitals as 'three-dimensional regions of maximum electron-finding probability', never as paths.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: ### 2. Orbital vs orbit  ·  • Orbit (Bohr): fixed two-dimensional circular path with definite radius and energy.  ·  • Orbital (quantum mechanics): three-dimensional probability distribution — spherical (s) or directional (p, d) — with no definite path and no sharp edge.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: $$\text{radial nodes}=n-1\ (s);\qquad P(r)=4\pi r^{2}|\psi|^{2}\ (\text{radial probability})$$  ·  ❌ s orbitals become dumbbell-shaped in higher shells. ✅ All s orbitals stay spherical; only size and nodes change with n.  ·  ❌ px, py and pz have different energies in an isolated atom. ✅ They are degenerate; a magnetic or ligand field is needed to split them.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ The electron stays inside the drawn boundary. ✅ The surface is a probability contour; there is a small chance of finding it outside.  ·  ❌ Arrows in the same box may point the same way. ✅ Pauli forbids it — opposite spins only.  ·  ❌ Pairing starts in the first p box. ✅ Hund's rule: each degenerate box gets one electron first.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Spin affects the shape of orbitals. ✅ Spin changes capacity and magnetism, not the shape given by l.  ·  ❌ 2s is just a bigger 1s. ✅ 2s also has an inner radial node and a second probability maximum — qualitatively different.  ·  ❌ The electron sits on the surface of the drawn sphere. ✅ The sphere is a probability boundary; the density decays continuously outward.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ s orbitals can be directional after hybridisation. ✅ Pure s is spherical; directionality appears only in hybrid orbitals (sp, sp², sp³).  ·  **Problem:** Compare the probability of finding the 1s electron at r = a₀ and r = 0. **Solution:** the *radial probability* 4πr²|ψ|² vanishes at r = 0 (the r² factor) and peaks at a₀ — even though |ψ|² itself is largest at the nucleus; the two curves answer different questions.  ·  Stay within s and p shapes for this syllabus; d and f are mentioned only as more complex.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Always draw boxes for degenerate orbitals separately; merging them loses the Hund's rule marks.  ·  Relate unpaired-electron count directly to magnetic behaviour in the answer.  ·  Distinguish |ψ|² (probability density, maximal at the nucleus for 1s) from radial probability (maximal at a₀) — a classic subtlety.
